newsitem.title: USA: Brennan was liberal conscience of U.S. high court.
newsitem.headline: Brennan was liberal conscience of U.S. high court.

text.p: Former U.S. Supreme Court Justice William Brennan, who died on Thursday after a long illness, was a towering liberal conscience on the court who fought more than three decades for the rights of the poor, minorities and women.
Brennan was 91. He retired from the court in 1990 after nearly 34 years as the architect of some of the most important decisions of his generation on civil rights and social reform.
He was one of the high court's intellectual legends and a master behind-the-scenes strategist.

"No individual, on or off the court, has had a more profound and sustained impact upon public policy in the United States," the conservative National Review magazine once said of Brennan, a stalwart liberal on the nine-member court.

On the court, Brennan played a key role in the liberal majority during the tumultuous period of American civil rights discord in the late 1950s and 1960s. Working with his liberal friend, Chief Justice Earl Warren, he wrote rulings that transformed constitutional law and ushered in social reform.

Brennan's decisions in civil rights cases enforced strict school desegregation plans, upheld affirmative action programmes designed to help minorities overcome past discrimination and sought to secure constitutional equality for women.

In criminal law, he opposed the death penalty, gave criminal suspects the right to have a lawyer present at police identification lineups and fought efforts to ease restrictions on the police during searches and seizures of evidence.

He also wrote important opinions that struck down state aid to religious schools, gave the press broad protection from libel suits, established rights for welfare recipients and illegal aliens and created the "one-man, one-vote" rule for representatation in voting districts.

As the court became more conservative in the 1970s and 1980s under Chief Justices Warren Burger and William Rehnquist, Brennan still exerted strong influence as the leader of the liberal wing. But he also found himself increasingly in the minority, writing in dissent.
For example, Brennan voted against the death penalty in every case that came before the court. In his view it violated the constitutional ban on cruel and unusual punishment.
Brennan maintained that position without wavering even though the court majority reinstated the death penalty in 1976 and polls showed a majority of the public favoured it.
"The calculated killing of a human being by the state involves, by its very nature, an absolute denial of the executed person's humanity," he said in a speech in 1985.
"The most vile murder does not, in my view, release the state from constitutional restraints on the destruction of human dignity."
Despite being in the minority in the late 1980s, Brennan often was able to muster enough votes for his position.
He was appointed to the Supreme Court in 1956 by President Dwight Eisenhower, who later regretted the decision.

The Republican Eisenhower had a bipartisan policy of appointing distinguished and moderate appellate court judges. Brennan, an Irish Catholic Democrat from New Jersey, seemed to fill that bill admirably.

But Eisenhower soon became dismayed with the new justice's liberal rulings. Asked if he had ever made a mistake as president, Eisenhower replied, "Yes, two; and they are both sitting on the Supreme Court" -- a reference to Brennan and the equally liberal Warren, whom Eisenhower appointed in 1953.
Brennan was born in Newark, N.J., on April 25, 1906, the second of eight children whose parents were Irish immigrants.
He graduated from the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School of Business in 1928 and earned his law degree from Harvard University three years later.
